Chapter 27

Async Svelte, and the getter trap

await inside $derived is wonderful, and it has one ordering rule that will cost you an afternoon if you do not know it.

By the end of this chapter

Use awaited deriveds confidently, and understand the server-rendering failure they can cause.

With experimental.async on, $derived can await. The terminal page reads almost like a synchronous script that happens to talk to a database:

Five lines that fetch from the server, pick a default, follow the URL, subscribe to a stream, and re-run precisely the parts that depend on what changed. In Kit 2 that is a load function, a $: block, a store subscription and an onDestroy.

There used to be a sixth, for positions. Where it went, and why, is the last section of this chapter.

The trap

Here is the error that started the afternoon:

The line it points at is the bind:value={ticket.price} on the ticket's price input. ticket is a $state object declared further down the script. On the client everything worked perfectly. Only server rendering died.

What is actually happening

When a component binds to a member of a $state object — ticket.side rather than a plain side variable — Svelte compiles a getter for it. During server rendering, everything after the first awaited $derived runs in a later microtask, but that getter runs in the first pass. So if ticket is declared below the awaited deriveds, the getter reads a variable that has not been initialised yet, and you get undefined.side.

The fix is one of the most anticlimactic in this course: move the declaration up.

The // … is three more $state declarations — lastSent, cancelError and ticketOpen — and seenPhase, a plain variable the next section uses. Only after all of them does the first await appear.

What makes this so easy to walk into is the asymmetry. bind:value={quantity} on a plain $state variable is completely fine in any order. It is only bind:value={ticket.quantity} — a member of a state object — that emits the getter. So you can have twenty bindings working and add the twenty-first, which happens to be a member access, and the page stops rendering on the server with an error pointing at a line you did not change.

The rule to carry: in a component with awaited $deriveds, declare all $state first. It costs nothing, it reads better anyway — state at the top, computed below — and it makes the ordering hazard impossible rather than merely avoided.

When to reach for $effect instead

One more piece of the terminal, because it draws the line between the two:

The test is simple. Does it produce a value the markup reads? $derived. Does it *do something* — animate, log, focus, start a timer? $effect. Deriveds are allowed to run more often than you expect, because they are cached and pure; effects are not, because they are neither.

The seenPhase !== null guard is the same class of thinking as the idempotent projectors: it separates "the state changed" from "this is the first time I am seeing state at all". Arriving at a market that is already open is not the market opening, and firing the venue's one dramatic animation at everybody who loads the page would make it mean nothing.

Where you await is what fails with it

An awaited $derived in the script is a promise the whole component waits on. On the server, if it rejects, the render has failed: there is no page to send, only the error page. That is the right trade for the instrument list, without which there is no terminal. It was the wrong one for positions.

A venue operator can open the terminal: the nav offers it, because watching the book and the tape is half the job. But an operator belongs to the venue, not to a member firm, holds no positions, and is refused view_positions. With getMyPositions() awaited in the script, that one refusal failed the page, and the operator lost the book, the tape and every Cancel button to a panel they had no use for.

The first fix moved the await into the markup, inside a <svelte:boundary>, and let the boundary catch the 403. On screen it looked right — the whole terminal, and a Positions panel saying "Your role does not allow that." Then somebody looked at the response: HTTP 403, for a page that had rendered perfectly. SvelteKit hands every boundary a transformError that runs the error through handleError and then sets the page's error and status from it — on the server and in the browser alike — so page.status read 403 too, and any monitor or client checking the status saw a failed page. A refusal you know is coming is not an error to catch. It is a branch.

This is the one job a load function still does best here: decide something about the page before any of it renders. The admin screen works the same way, with data.canSeeQueue ? await getQueue() : null. The panel then branches, and keeps a boundary for what nobody can predict:

A <svelte:boundary> catches what fails inside it, during rendering or in an await, and shows its failed snippet instead of its contents. Everything outside carries on. So a dropped connection or a fault at our end now costs this panel and nothing else — though, as above, it still sets the page's status, which for a genuine fault is honest.

Why the await is in the markup, not the script

Because the server and the browser must agree. On the server a script-level $derived(await …) that rejects fails the render before any boundary in the markup exists to catch it, and the person gets the error page. In the browser, after a client-side navigation, a boundary around the place the value is *read* does catch it — which is how an earlier version of this test suite passed with the await still in the script: it only ever reached the terminal by navigating there after signing in. Written inside the boundary, the await fails inside the boundary in both places. The browser test now reloads the page as the operator and asserts a 200, so the server's half is checked too.

No pending snippet, and a retry that refreshes

The boundary has a failed snippet and deliberately no pending one. Svelte's documentation: "During server-side rendering, a boundary with a pending snippet renders that snippet and ignores the rest of its content" — so a pending snippet would make every first load show a placeholder where the server could have sent the table. And the retry is offered only for a fault (a status of 500 or more), because a refusal answers the same way every time. It calls getMyPositions().refresh() before reset(): reset re-renders the boundary's contents, but a query that failed keeps its failure until it is refreshed, so on its own the retry would await the same rejection again. A browser test drops the connection on that one request, checks the panel says so while the rest of the terminal carries on, restores it, and presses Try again.

The error is an App.Error, and the cast says so

What reaches failed under SvelteKit is not the thing that was thrown. Kit puts every boundary's error through its error handling first — the server's handleError for a query that called error(...), the client-side handleError (Kit's default here, as there is no hooks.client.ts) for anything thrown in the browser — and passes on the result: an App.Error, a plain { status, message } object, plus the id our handleError adds to unexpected errors. A runtime probe that forced a query to throw error(418, 'probe query') printed {"instanceofError":false,"ctor":"Object","keys":["status","message"],"message":"probe query","status":418} — the same on the server render and after a client-side navigation. Svelte itself types the parameter unknown, because a boundary in plain Svelte can catch anything at all, and the strict checker rejects annotating it as App.Error. So the snippet says it once, in a declaration tag: {const failure = $derived(error as App.Error)}. The cast is not a guess but a statement of what Kit guarantees, and the comment above the boundary says so.

That line is a declaration tag — {const …} in the markup, scoped to the block it sits in — and it is the current way to name a value inside a template. The legacy spelling was {@const failure = …}, which Svelte's documentation now calls "considered legacy — use declaration tags instead". Unlike {@const}, a declaration tag is an ordinary declaration, so it is reactive only if you ask: "When values should be reactive, you can use $state and $derived." That is why it says $derived — the snippet is the same failed snippet for every failure, and the name should follow whichever error it was handed. Chapter 35 meets the other declaration tag on this page.

And the failure the panel cannot absorb — a page whose load refuses, a route that does not exist — goes to src/routes/+error.svelte, which receives the same App.Error as a prop:

Three headings, because three different things happened: the venue failed, the page is not there, or the venue refused for a reason it states. Only the first gets a Try again button — a reload cannot change a refusal or conjure a missing page, and offering one says it might.

ErrorProps comes from ./$types, the module svelte-kit sync generates for each route folder — the reason chapter 22 put .svelte-kit/types in the tsconfig. Every page and layout in Sequent types its props the same way: let { data }: PageProps = $props() on a page, LayoutProps on a layout. That makes data exactly what the route's load returned, so a field added to the load appears in the component and a field removed from it is a type error, where a hand-written { data: { … } } would have drifted silently — the layout's once said a viewer's role was any string, when the domain says it is one of five.

This file replaced a boundary in the root layout that wrapped every page, guarded its message with error instanceof Error, and had never once run. The guard was wrong — an App.Error is never an Error, so the fallback "We could not load this." would have won every time — but it did not matter, because SvelteKit 3 wraps each page in a boundary of its own that renders the nearest +error.svelte, falling back to Kit's built-in one when the app has none. The page's failure was always caught one level below the layout, and shown as Kit's bare status code and message. A boundary is only reached if nothing nearer catches first.

Checkpoint

  • You can use await inside $derived and explain what re-runs when
  • You can state the declaration-order rule and the exact error breaking it produces
  • You can explain why a plain $state binding is unaffected but a member binding is not
  • You can decide between $derived and $effect from what the code does, not how it looks
  • You can decide whether an await belongs in the script or inside a boundary, from what should fail with it, and why the server and the browser disagree when it is in the wrong place
  • You can explain why a refusal you can predict belongs in the load as a flag, not in a boundary — and what a caught error does to the page's status
  • You can say what a failed snippet and +error.svelte receive, and why the layout's boundary never ran
  • You can write a declaration tag, and say when it needs $derived
